explanations.answer: He directs it where He pleases
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (Proverbs 1:1), says the LORD directs the king's heart "…where He pleases." Picture a waterway: the water doesn't pick the route. Even the man wearing the crown has his heart in the LORD's hand.

explanations.answer: He lets it flow wherever it likes
explanations.explanation: I get the pull, friend, because free-flowing sounds relaxing. But Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (Proverbs 1:1), says the opposite. The king's heart is in the LORD's hand, and "He directs it where He pleases." The steering belongs to the LORD, not to the water.

explanations.answer: He leaves it to the king's advisors
explanations.explanation: Advisors can whisper all day long, friend. But Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (Proverbs 1:1), puts the king's heart in the hand of the LORD, not in the hands of the people around the throne. The verse says "He directs it where He pleases." Nobody else gets named.
Heart is the word, friend. A man can walk his own road feeling great about it, and verse 2 says the LORD weighs the heart. He's not only looking at what we did. He's looking at what's underneath it.

Hands is a fair guess, since hands are how we get things done. But verse 2 says the LORD weighs the heart. Hands show what we do, and the heart is the part underneath. That's a good reminder not to grade ourselves too quickly.
Words matter plenty in this chapter, friend. Verse 23 even talks about guarding your mouth and tongue. But in verse 2 the thing the LORD weighs is the heart.

Verse 3 flips that around, friend. It says, "To do righteousness and justice is more desirable to the LORD than sacrifice." I know a sacrifice looks impressive, but a big offering can't stand in for treating people right. The doing comes first, and the offering doesn't make up for skipping it.

Right, it goes the other way. The verse says, "To do righteousness and justice is more desirable to the LORD than sacrifice." Solomon puts the doing ahead of the offering. A gift with no righteous living behind it is like a cookie box with no cookies in it.
True, friend. Solomon says haughty eyes and a proud heart, the guides of the wicked, are sin. He doesn't call them a small slip. He just says sin, plain and simple.
Verse 4 actually says it straight, friend. Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the guides of the wicked, are sin. Solomon doesn't soften it. So the answer is True.

Poverty is it, friend. Solomon says the plans of the diligent bring plenty, "…as surely as haste leads to poverty." Careful plans on one side, rushing on the other. And he says it with total confidence.
Honor sounds nice, but that's not where verse 5 sends haste. Solomon says the plans of the diligent bring plenty, "…as surely as haste leads to poverty." Haste ends up in a pretty empty place.

A long life is a lovely thing, friend, but verse 5 doesn't tie it to haste. Solomon says the plans of the diligent bring plenty, "…as surely as haste leads to poverty." Rush a batch with no plan and you get a mess and an empty cookie box. Haste leads to poverty.
A vanishing mist, yes. Solomon says a fortune made by a lying tongue is a vanishing mist, a deadly pursuit. Like the steam off a fresh tray, you reach for it and your hand closes on nothing.

Heavy burden is a strong picture, friend, but it isn't the one Solomon picked. Verse 6 calls a fortune made by a lying tongue "…a vanishing mist…" Mist doesn't stay put, and you can't pack it in a box. Solomon also calls it a deadly pursuit.

Sharp sword sounds dramatic, friend, but verse 6 uses a softer picture. A fortune made by a lying tongue is "…a vanishing mist…" A sword you can at least hold, but mist slips right through your fingers. Solomon then adds that it's a deadly pursuit.

True, friend. Verse 7 says, "The violence of the wicked will sweep them away because they refuse to do what is just." The thing they do ends up carrying them off. It's a heavy line, so it's worth reading slowly.

This one is True, friend. Verse 7 says, "The violence of the wicked will sweep them away because they refuse to do what is just." It's all right there in the line. This one is heavy, so it's worth reading slowly.

Upright, friend. Verse 8 puts a crooked way next to the conduct of the innocent, which is upright. One road bends, and the other runs straight. Solomon sets them side by side so you can see the difference.
Verse 8 sets them side by side, friend, so they don't match. The way of a guilty man is crooked, "…but the conduct of the innocent is upright." The little word "but" is doing the work there.

Nothing in verse 8 says hidden, friend. Solomon says the way of a guilty man is crooked, "…but the conduct of the innocent is upright." A crooked way bends all over the place, and upright stands straight. The word he picks for the innocent is upright, not hidden.

explanations.answer: Sharing a house with a quarrelsome wife
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Verse 9 says a corner of the roof is better than sharing a house with a quarrelsome wife. That's how strongly Solomon puts it. He'd take the cramped roof corner over the house.

explanations.answer: Serving a king who is always angry
explanations.explanation: A king who's always angry sounds rough, friend, but verse 9 doesn't mention him. Solomon says a corner of the roof is better than sharing a house with a quarrelsome wife. That's the comparison he makes.

explanations.answer: Working a field in the summer heat
explanations.explanation: Summer heat sounds like a long day, friend, but no field shows up in verse 9. Solomon says a corner of the roof is better than sharing a house with a quarrelsome wife. A roof corner has no walls and no comfort, and he still picks it. I think that tells you how much he values a peaceful home.
Craves fits the first blank. Verse 10 says the soul of the wicked man craves evil. Solomon is showing us what the man wants way down inside.
Favor goes in the second blank. His neighbor "…finds no favor in his eyes." So the man doesn't look kindly on his neighbor. Solomon is showing how the wicked man sees the people around him.
Fears is a fair guess, friend, but verse 10 uses a different word. The soul of the wicked man craves evil. Solomon says what he wants, not what scares him.
Hates is a strong word, and verse 10 doesn't use it. The soul of the wicked man craves evil. The neighbor finds no favor, which is a different thing from hate.
Fault is a neat guess, friend, because it sounds like a man picking at his neighbor. But it's not in verse 10. The neighbor "…finds no favor in his eyes." Favor is the word Solomon picked.

Yes, friend. Verse 11 says when a mocker is punished, the simple gain wisdom. The punishment of the mocker is the moment Solomon names. The verse also says that when a wise man is instructed, he acquires knowledge.

A coronation is a big day, friend, but verse 11 doesn't mention one. It says the simple gain wisdom when a mocker is punished. That's the moment Solomon names. The second half says a wise man acquires knowledge when he is instructed.
Harvest time brings plenty of gains, friend, but verse 11 points somewhere else. The simple gain wisdom when a mocker is punished. That's the moment Solomon names.
True, friend. Verse 11 says, "…when a wise man is instructed, he acquires knowledge." Even the wise keep learning. Nobody graduates from it.
This one is True, friend. Verse 11 says, "…when a wise man is instructed, he acquires knowledge." A wise man who gets instructed picks up knowledge. Being wise doesn't turn off the learning.

Yes, friend. Verse 12 says the Righteous One considers the house of the wicked and brings the wicked to ruin. Notice the verse says He considers their house. It's a serious line, so it's worth taking in quietly.
Verse 12 doesn't say that, friend. It says the Righteous One considers the house of the wicked and brings the wicked to ruin. That's a heavy line.
Riches would be quite a turn, friend, but verse 12 goes the other direction. The Righteous One considers the house of the wicked and brings the wicked to ruin. This one is heavy.

explanations.answer: He too will cry out with no answer
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Verse 13 says whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor, "…he too shall cry out and receive no answer." The very thing he did comes back around to him.

explanations.answer: He will find honor in the end
explanations.explanation: Honor is a nice thing to hope for, friend, but verse 13 says something else. Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor, "…he too shall cry out and receive no answer." Honor isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: He will keep all his wealth
explanations.explanation: Keeping his wealth isn't what the verse says, friend. Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor, "…he too shall cry out and receive no answer." Solomon doesn't mention wealth at all.
Secret, friend. Verse 14 says a gift in secret soothes anger. That's what Solomon observes about calming someone's anger. The verse adds that a covert bribe pacifies great wrath.
Public is a fair guess, friend, but verse 14 uses the opposite word. It says a gift in secret soothes anger. The giving happens out of sight.

Return sounds like it fits, friend, because a gift for a gift feels natural. But it isn't in verse 14. The line says a gift in secret soothes anger. Secret is the word, so the giving happens out of sight.
A terror, friend. Verse 15 says justice executed is a joy to the righteous, "…but a terror to the workers of iniquity." The same justice lands very differently on each side.

A warning is a gentle word, friend, but verse 15 reaches for a stronger one. Justice executed is a joy to the righteous, "…but a terror to the workers of iniquity." So why does the same justice land so differently? Verse 7 says the violence of the wicked will sweep them away "…because they refuse to do what is just." I think that's the split: the righteous are on the side of justice, and the workers of iniquity are the ones refusing it.

A lesson is a tidy guess, friend, but verse 15 isn't that mild. Justice executed is a joy to the righteous, "…but a terror to the workers of iniquity." A lesson is something you calmly take notes on. Terror is what you feel when you've been working against what's right. I think Solomon wants you to see how differently the same justice lands.
Verse 16 says it differently, friend, and this one is heavy. The man who strays from the path of understanding will rest in the assembly of the dead. It says the dead, not the living.
Right, friend. This one is heavy. Verse 16 says the man who strays from the path of understanding will rest in the assembly of the dead, not the living. The statement swaps in the wrong word.
Poor, friend. Verse 17 says he who loves pleasure will become poor. Loving pleasure ends up draining the pockets. The verse adds that the one who loves wine and oil will never be rich.
Lonely is a sad thing, friend, but verse 17 names a different result. He who loves pleasure will become poor. Solomon is talking about money here.

Lazy fits the mood of the chapter, friend, since verse 25 talks about the slacker. But verse 17 says he who loves pleasure will become poor. Solomon names poverty here, and the verse adds that the one who loves wine and oil will never be rich. I think the two warnings sit close together, because chasing pleasure and refusing work both end up with empty pockets. Still, this verse is about the pleasure.
Verse 18 says it the other way around, friend. It says, "The wicked become a ransom for the righteous, and the faithless for the upright." So the wicked are the ransom, not the righteous.
Right, it's reversed. Verse 18 says, "The wicked become a ransom for the righteous, and the faithless for the upright." The wicked are the ransom there, not the righteous. That's a tough line.

Consumes, friend. Verse 20 says precious treasures and oil are in the dwelling of the wise, "…but a foolish man consumes them." The wise have it stored up, and the fool gets through it. Treasure on one side, consuming on the other.

Hiding things away is a careful move, friend, but verse 20 says something else. Precious treasures and oil are in the dwelling of the wise, "…but a foolish man consumes them." Consumes is the word. Think of a cookie jar that's empty by Tuesday.
Guarding sounds like the wise man's move, friend. Verse 20 says precious treasures and oil are in the dwelling of the wise, "…but a foolish man consumes them." The fool uses it all up.
Verse 22 goes the other way, friend. A wise man scales the city of the mighty and pulls down the stronghold in which they trust. The stronghold doesn't stay standing.
False is right, friend. Verse 22 says a wise man scales the city of the mighty and pulls down the stronghold in which they trust. The thing they leaned on comes down.
Distress, friend. Verse 23 says he who guards his mouth and tongue keeps his soul from distress. A watched tongue saves a lot of trouble. Solomon ties the mouth straight to the soul.
Anger is a fair guess, friend, since tongues stir it up plenty. But verse 23 says he who guards his mouth and tongue keeps his soul from distress. Distress is the word.

Hunger doesn't show up in verse 23, friend. It says he who guards his mouth and tongue keeps his soul from distress. You know that moment when you hit send on a message and wish you could grab it back? That's the kind of distress a guarded tongue can spare.
Yes, friend. Verse 25 says the craving of the slacker kills him because his hands refuse to work. Notice the because: his hands refuse to work. It's a sober line.
Riches would be nice, friend, but verse 25 says the opposite. The craving of the slacker kills him because his hands refuse to work. He wants, but won't work.
Wisdom would be a happy ending, friend, but verse 25 doesn't give it. The craving of the slacker kills him because his hands refuse to work. It's a heavy line.
True, friend. Verse 26 says all day long he covets more, "…but the righteous give without restraint." One keeps coveting more, and the other gives. Solomon puts them side by side.
This one is True, friend. Verse 26 says all day long he covets more, "…but the righteous give without restraint." The righteous aren't holding back.

explanations.answer: When it's brought with ill intent
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Verse 27 says the sacrifice of the wicked is detestable, "…how much more so when brought with ill intent!" The intent makes it worse.
Timing is a smart thing to wonder about, friend, but verse 27 doesn't mention it. The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable, "…how much more so when brought with ill intent!" Ill intent is the thing.

explanations.answer: When it's brought by a stranger
explanations.explanation: A stranger isn't in the picture here, friend. Verse 27 says the sacrifice of the wicked is detestable, "…how much more so when brought with ill intent!" It's already detestable, and ill intent makes it even more so. Who carries it isn't part of the verse.

True, friend. Verse 28 says a lying witness will perish, "…but the man who listens to truth will speak forever." The liar's words die with him, but the listener's words last. I think that's worth remembering: the one who listens well ends up with the word that outlives everybody else's.
This one is True, friend. Verse 28 says a lying witness will perish, "…but the man who listens to truth will speak forever." It sets the liar and the listener side by side.

Sure, friend. Verse 29 says a wicked man hardens his face, "…but the upright man makes his way sure." One goes stiff and stubborn, and the other goes steady. I think the difference is that a hard face has stopped listening, while a sure way keeps moving forward.
Verse 29 draws a line between them, friend, so they don't match. A wicked man hardens his face, "…but the upright man makes his way sure." The upright man has a different path.

Hiding isn't in verse 29, friend. It says a wicked man hardens his face, "…but the upright man makes his way sure." The upright man isn't ducking out of sight. I think a sure way is the opposite of hiding, because he's walking out in the open with nothing to dodge.

True, friend. Verse 30 says, "There is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel that can prevail against the LORD." Nothing on that list gets past Him. Wisdom, understanding and counsel all fall short against the LORD.
This one is True, friend. Verse 30 says, "There is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel that can prevail against the LORD." Not even the smartest plan in the room.

The LORD, friend. Verse 31 says, "A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD." Getting the horse ready is a good thing to do, and the verse doesn't say to skip it. But the preparing and the victory are two different jobs, and the victory belongs to the LORD.

A king gets a lot of credit, friend, but verse 31 doesn't give him this one. It says, "A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD." Even a king can get the horse ready, and that's as far as his part goes in this verse. The victory is the LORD's, and I think that keeps everybody humble, crown or no crown.

Brave soldiers get plenty of cheers, friend, but verse 31 sends the victory somewhere else. It says, "A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD." All the preparing in the world, the horse and the courage included, still isn't the same as the victory. The verse keeps that for the LORD alone.
